analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal national health insurance program funded by a new value-added tax.
analysis.headline: Dingell's bill to cover every American through a national health insurance program died in House committee with zero cosponsors and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made medical, dental, hospital, nursing, and certain other services available to nearly everyone, paid from a National Health Care Trust Fund financed by a new value-added tax on commercial transactions. Patients would choose their own doctors and hospitals, doctors would keep wide practice freedom, and states or local committees would administer the program. Medicare recipients would get whatever services Medicare didn't cover, and the program would eventually absorb Medicare. It was referred to two House committees and two subcommittees, gained no cosponsors, and died there when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, virtually every American would have gained health coverage regardless of employment, income, or health status, with no premiums or networks: the bill makes medical, dental, podiatric, home-nursing, hospital, and auxiliary services available to eligible individuals and allows patients free choice of physician and hospital [S3]. Uninsured needy individuals would be covered using existing Medicaid-related federal grants [S3]. The bill prohibits discrimination based on race, creed, or color in who receives services and who may participate as a provider [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Eligibility runs on work-history quarters (or receipt of Social Security or civil service benefits), with dependents covered, so coverage follows work and family rather than a specific employer [S3].
Patients may freely choose and change their physician, dentist, hospital, or medical group, and emergency and other cases can bypass referral requirements [S3].

Providers are protected too: doctors, dentists, and nurses keep freedom to practice where they choose and to accept or reject patients consistent with state law and professional ethics, and hospitals keep control over their own administration [S3].
Funding comes from a dedicated National Health Care Trust Fund supplied by a value-added tax, with the tax set at zero for retail food, housing, and medical care [S3].

Medicare beneficiaries would get covered for services Medicare doesn't pay for, including covering Medicare's deductibles and coinsurance gaps, and the Secretary would study transferring Medicare fully into the new program [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Buyers and sellers of taxable goods and services would pay the new value-added tax, which businesses would collect; the private health insurance industry would lose its core business, since the public fund would replace most private coverage; hospitals would face regulated payment at reasonable cost with possible maximum rates, and doctors would have their payment methods and rates set through state agreements rather than private negotiation [S3].

drawbacks.text: The value-added tax is a broad consumption tax on commercial transactions; even with food, housing, and medical care zero-rated, it would raise prices on most other purchases and fall hardest on households that spend a large share of income [S3].

Hospital coverage is capped at 60 days per benefit year, and the National Health Insurance Board may limit dental, home-nursing, and auxiliary services if personnel, facilities, or funds are inadequate — an explicit rationing authority [S3].
Doctors may still reject patients under state law and professional ethics, so access in some areas could remain uneven despite universal eligibility [S3].
The bill contains no estimate of the tax rate or total program cost, leaving the financing burden unquantified at introduction [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered universal, choice-preserving health coverage funded by a dedicated tax, which is a genuine and large gain for ordinary people — especially the uninsured. But the costs were real and unquantified: a broad new consumption tax, a 60-day hospital cap, and a Board empowered to restrict dental and other services if money ran short. It was a sweeping redesign whose tradeoffs were never examined in any hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee and subcommittee from its second week onward, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell introduced the National Health Insurance Act on January 6, 1999 [S1][S5].

The House referred it to the Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and eleven days later it was sent to the Health and Environment subcommittee of Commerce and the Health subcommittee of Ways and Means [S5].
No further action of any kind was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo, above all the private health insurance industry, which kept its market intact; no American gained coverage from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors signed on from either party, and both committees of referral were chaired by Republicans in the 106th Congress, so the bill never drew a recorded partisan vote to measure support.

industries.note: The bill replaces employer-based and individually purchased coverage with a publicly financed trust fund, eliminating most of the private insurance market; it allows insurers to serve only as administrative agents for state plans. Their gain from the bill's failure is the public's continued exposure to premiums, deductibles, and denials.

Hospitals would gain guaranteed payment from a universal patient pool — ending uncompensated care — but payment would be based on reasonable cost with possible maximum rates set by regulation. Universal coverage expands the pool of paying patients they treat.

The bill guarantees physicians fee-for-service, capitation, or salary payment options, protects their choice of locality, and preserves their right to accept or reject patients — but payment rates and methods would be negotiated through state agencies rather than set privately. Most would gain a universally covered patient population while losing billing autonomy.

industries.industry: Businesses subject to the value-added tax
industries.note: Commercial transactions would bear a new tax that sellers must collect, raising the cost of taxable goods and services — though food, housing, and medical care are exempt. Many employers would simultaneously be relieved of health insurance premiums.
